name: DigitalUndivided BIG (Black Innovation Grant) Program
description: The DigitalUndivided Black Innovation Grant (BIG) Program awards $5,000 grants to Black and Latina women small-business owners whose businesses incorporate a technology component. The program supports entrepreneurs who have been in business for at least one year and demonstrate annual revenue of at least $50,000. BIG recipients also receive access to mentorship, business development resources, and a peer community of fellow women tech entrepreneurs. The program is designed to close the funding gap faced by women of color in the startup ecosystem and help scale businesses that drive economic impact in their communities.
eligibility: Black or Latina women business owners with at least 1 year in business, minimum $50,000 annual revenue, and a technology component in their business model; must be US-based
applicationProcess: Apply online through the digitalundivided website during the open application period. Applicants must submit a business profile, revenue documentation, and a description of the technology component of their business. Finalists may be invited for an interview or pitch session. Awards are announced on a rolling basis.
documentsRequired: Proof of business ownership; revenue documentation (tax returns or financial statements showing $50,000+ annual revenue); business plan or pitch deck; proof of technology component; personal identification

name: Qredits PAFMI Migrant Entrepreneur Training and Microloans (Netherlands)
organization: Qredits / Council of Europe Development Bank (CEB)
description: The PAFMI (Pathway to Integration and Entrepreneurship for Migrants) program is a €3.5 million initiative implemented by the Council of Europe Development Bank and financed by the EU's Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF). In the Netherlands, Qredits — a leading social microfinance institution — delivers the program by organizing entrepreneurial training programs for migrants, combined with access to microloans for those who complete the training and develop viable business plans. The program has organized 18 entrepreneurial training cohorts across the Netherlands, helping migrants overcome barriers to starting their own businesses such as language, regulatory unfamiliarity, and lack of access to traditional financing. Participants receive business coaching, financial literacy education, and networking opportunities alongside loan access.
eligibility: Migrants and refugees residing in the Netherlands who want to start or grow a small business; participants must complete the entrepreneurial training program; no minimum credit score required
amount: Microloans up to €50,000 through Qredits; training provided free of charge
applicationProcess: Contact Qredits (qredits.nl) or local partner organizations to register for the next PAFMI training cohort. Complete the multi-week entrepreneurial training program covering business planning, financial management, Dutch regulatory requirements, and marketing. Upon successful completion and with a viable business plan, apply for a Qredits microloan. Business coaching continues after loan disbursement.
geographicScope: Netherlands — training cohorts held in multiple cities across the country
documentsRequired: Valid residence permit in the Netherlands; proof of migration status; business concept or plan (developed during training); personal identification; proof of address

name: International Entrepreneur Parole (IEP) — USCIS
description: The International Entrepreneur Parole (IEP) rule allows the Department of Homeland Security to grant parole to foreign entrepreneurs who demonstrate that their presence in the United States would provide a significant public benefit. Eligible entrepreneurs must have a substantial ownership stake in a startup entity that was recently formed in the United States and that has substantial and demonstrated potential for rapid growth and job creation. The program provides an initial stay of up to 30 months, with the possibility of a re-parole period of up to 30 additional months. While not a visa or grant in the traditional sense, IEP provides the legal framework for immigrant founders to remain in the US to build their companies, and is often paired with venture capital, angel investment, or government grants that the startup has received.
eligibility: Foreign national entrepreneurs who possess at least a 10% ownership stake in a startup formed in the US within the past 5 years; startup must have received at least $264,147 in qualifying government grants or awards, OR at least $264,147 in capital from qualified US investors; entrepreneur must have a central and active role in the startup
amount: No direct funding — provides legal authorization to stay in the US; startup must demonstrate $264,147+ in qualifying investment or government grants
applicationProcess: File Form I-941 (Application for Entrepreneur Parole) with USCIS along with supporting evidence of qualifying investment, government funding, or alternative criteria demonstrating substantial public benefit. USCIS reviews applications on a case-by-case basis. If approved, parole is granted for up to 30 months with possibility of re-parole for an additional 30 months. Spouses may apply for work authorization.
geographicScope: United States — nationwide; entrepreneur must operate the startup within US territory
documentsRequired: Form I-941; evidence of startup formation (articles of incorporation, EIN); proof of ownership stake (≥10%); evidence of qualifying investment or government awards (≥$264,147); business plan; personal identification and passport; evidence of entrepreneur's central role in the company

name: Pursuit Lending Small Business Loans for Immigrants
description: Pursuit is a Community Development Financial Institution (CDFI) and SBA-preferred lender that provides small business loans specifically designed for underserved communities, including immigrant business owners. Operating primarily in the New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Pennsylvania region, Pursuit offers SBA-backed loans, microloans, and lines of credit to entrepreneurs who may face barriers with traditional banks due to limited credit history, language challenges, or immigration status. Pursuit provides bilingual support, business advisory services, and flexible underwriting criteria that consider the entrepreneur's full story rather than just credit scores. The organization has deployed over $2.5 billion in financing to more than 37,000 small businesses, with a strong focus on minority and immigrant entrepreneurs.
eligibility: Small business owners and entrepreneurs in the NY/NJ/CT/PA region; immigrants and minorities are specifically served; must have a viable business plan; no strict minimum credit score; business must be located in Pursuit's service area
amount: Microloans from $500 to $50,000; SBA loans up to $5.5 million; lines of credit available
applicationProcess: Apply online through pursuitlending.com or visit one of Pursuit's regional offices. Complete the loan application with business and personal financial information. A Pursuit loan officer will review the application and may request additional documentation. Bilingual support is available in Spanish. Business advisory services are offered alongside the loan to help ensure success.
geographicScope: New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Pennsylvania
documentsRequired: Business plan or description; personal identification; tax returns (personal and business if available); bank statements; proof of business ownership; lease agreement or proof of business location

name: Dutch Startup Visa — Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO)
organization: Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO) / Immigration and Naturalisation Service (IND)
description: The Dutch Startup Visa is a Netherlands government program designed to attract innovative entrepreneurs from outside the European Union. The visa allows non-EU entrepreneurs to reside in the Netherlands for one year while developing their startup idea under the guidance of an approved Dutch facilitator (incubator, accelerator, or mentor). During this period, entrepreneurs have access to the Dutch startup ecosystem, co-working spaces, networking events, and business development support through their facilitator. After the initial year, entrepreneurs who have demonstrated sufficient progress can transition to a self-employment residence permit to continue growing their business in the Netherlands. The program requires no minimum investment and is specifically designed for early-stage founders with innovative business concepts.
eligibility: Non-EU/EEA entrepreneurs with an innovative product or service idea; must partner with an approved Dutch facilitator (listed on RVO website); must have sufficient financial means to support themselves during the year (approximately €1,400/month); must meet standard immigration requirements
amount: No direct funding — provides 1-year residence permit; facilitators may provide workspace, mentoring, and connections to investors
applicationProcess: 1) Find and partner with an approved Dutch facilitator from the RVO register. 2) The facilitator submits a startup facilitation agreement to RVO for assessment. 3) Once RVO issues a positive assessment, apply for the startup visa at the Dutch embassy or consulate in your home country. 4) Upon arrival, begin developing your startup with facilitator guidance. 5) Before the 1-year visa expires, apply for a self-employment residence permit if you wish to continue.
geographicScope: Netherlands — nationwide; facilitators available in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague, Eindhoven, and other cities
documentsRequired: Valid passport; signed startup facilitation agreement with approved Dutch facilitator; RVO positive assessment letter; proof of sufficient financial means (€1,400/month); health insurance covering the Netherlands; clean criminal record certificate; passport photos
